narrative:
The model estimated a 57.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is a higher failure risk than the school was willing to accept, your application was rejected. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty about your ability.

The strongest factor in the decision was your year-three class-standing decile. A value of 1 is far below the accepted-student average of about 5.8, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score. It was treated as a relative strength that pushed toward passing, but your score of 34 remains below the accepted average of 37.18. The third factor was your year-one decile, also 1 versus an accepted average near 6.0; it pushed toward failure as well. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 versus an average of 3.23, middle-income background, and full-time status were not the main drivers.

To improve a future application, seek admissions advising about these concerns, prepare for and consider retaking the LSAT, and provide context or additional evidence of academic readiness. Ask what steps would demonstrate a lower bar-exam risk before reapplying.
